title: Raga Gauri
hookLine: the largest section of the Granth (ang 151), earnest and deep

cards: Last thing at night, in the Sohila, the first hymn carries a heading that's easy to pass right over: Raag Gauri Deepaki. So anyone who has read the bedtime prayer has already seen Gauri named. Its main home is further on.
On ang one hundred fifty-one the Gauri section begins, and then it keeps going, page after page after page. The book names a mood, and then stays inside it for a long walk.

teach.b: Gauri is the raga of the serious conversation. Musical tradition hears it as earnest and deep, a mood for things that matter and won't be rushed: not grief, exactly, and not joy, but attention.
And Gauri comes in shades. The section opens with Gauri Guarairi.

Turn the pages and you'll find Gauri Purbi, Gauri Bairagan, Gauri Cheti, Gauri Majh, Gauri Deepaki, each a different color of the same raga, written above the hymns it carries. One deep voice, many tones.
Nor is it one speaker. The Gurus' hymns fill the first long stretch. Then Kabir's hymns in Gauri fill a long stretch of their own, with Namdev and Ravidas after.
One taste of the earnestness: a hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur in Gauri, on ang two hundred nineteen.

teach.h: GIVE UP THE PRIDE OF THE MIND.
teach.b: O holy ones, it says in paraphrase, give up the pride of the mind. Run, day and night, from lust and anger and bad company. No ornament, just a plain instruction from someone who means it.
That's the Gauri sound: no hurry, no show, a voice leaning in close to say the true thing.
Why so much of the Granth in this one raga? The text doesn't say, and it's fine to leave the question open.
But so much of what the Gurus said about the mind, pride, the Name, death and peace found a home in a raga built for saying serious things. Tomorrow, two great compositions that live here.

how: Gauri hymns are sung in kirtan in the raga named in their headings, and Sikhs who say the Kirtan Sohila at night meet Gauri in its first hymn, headed Raag Gauri Deepaki.

o: a bright raga for weddings and feasts
a raga used only for the evening prayer
an earnest, deep raga with a long section

p: the first hymn of the Sohila
the shade that opens the section
give up the pride of the mind

s: Gauri appears only in its own section of the Granth
the Sohila's first hymn, said at night, is headed Raag Gauri Deepaki.
Gauri's headings name several shades of the raga
Gauri Guarairi, Purbi, Bairagan, Cheti, Majh, Deepaki and more.
Gauri is heard as a light, playful raga
musical tradition hears it as earnest and deep.

games.q: you have something serious to say about pride, the mind and death. which voice do you choose?
o: an earnest, unhurried raga like Gauri.
games.why: page after page of the Granth's serious teaching stands in Gauri, a raga heard as earnest and deep.

practice: If you can find a shabad in Raag Gauri, play it and listen for the earnestness before the words, a melody that leans in rather than shows off.

Otherwise, sit up a little straighter and let one serious thing come to mind, a choice, a worry, a person, giving it your full attention without arguing or solving, and come back without scolding when the mind wanders.
If you pray, set that one serious thing beside a quiet Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Raga Gauri. The third raga section of the Granth, beginning on ang one hundred fifty-one and running on for page after page, in many named shades, heard as earnest and deep. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, as the headings spell it: Gauri, the raga of the Granth's third section.

carryVoice: Your line: earnest and deep. Gauri is a raga built for saying serious things, without hurry. Until tomorrow.
